slides.title: Why a thin film
bullets: Examination of a blood film lets you assess the quantitative and morphological details of leukocytes and erythrocytes; a thin film is examined in leukocytosis, anaemia and similar conditions.
The film is fixed in alcohol to preserve the red cells intact and allow their morphology to be assessed.
Morphological assessment of cells is subjective: it depends largely on how well the film was made and on the experience of the worker.
A good thin film takes skill: a thick film has ragged edges and streaks, the red cells are altered and the leukocytes gather at the edges.

slides.title: Materials and reagents
bullets: A sterile lancet or needle, cotton wool, 70% ethyl alcohol, a plastic pear-shaped pipette.
Clean, unscratched microscope slides, a ground-edge spreader slide, a wax pencil.
For fixing: methyl alcohol (ethyl alcohol is possible), which must be water-free; a dropper bottle.

slides.title: Materials and reagents
bullets: For staining: a freshly prepared 10% Romanowsky–Giemsa working solution, buffered water (pH 6.8–7.2), a timer, forceps, a rack for staining and drying.

slides.title: Making the film
bullets: 1. Number the slides and check that the number matches the one on the patient’s card.
2. Wipe the finger with alcohol and let it dry; puncture the side of the third or fourth finger with a sterile lancet and wipe off the first drop.
3. Squeeze the finger gently, take the next drop with a plastic pipette and place it in the middle of the slide 1–2 cm from the edge; there should be little blood.

slides.title: Making the film
bullets: 4. Place the spreader at 30–45° about 1–2 mm in front of the drop and draw it back until it touches the drop — the blood spreads along the corners of the two slides.
5. Then push the spreader with one smooth movement to the end of the slide (without pressing hard); the blood runs out before it reaches the edge.
6. The film should be 3–4 cm long; leave it to dry completely in the open air.

slides.title: Judging the film
bullets: The film should not be thick.
There should be no ragged edges and no lengthwise or crosswise streaks.
There should be no empty patches (a sign that the slide was not properly degreased).
A correctly made dry film is thin, yellowish and ends 1–1.5 cm from the edge.
If the volume of blood is always the same and it is spread evenly on the same part of the slide, staining and reading are standardised — hence the pear-shaped pipette.

slides.title: Fixation and staining
bullets: 1. Put the dry film on the staining support, apply 2–3 drops of alcohol and fix it for 2–3 minutes.
2. Pour off the excess alcohol; dry the film completely in air before staining.
3. Pour the stain slowly over the whole film; start the timer and stain for 10 minutes.

slides.title: Fixation and staining
bullets: 4. Lift the slide with forceps and wash the stain off gently with buffered water holding it at a slant; repeat 2–3 times.
5. Put the film in the drying rack and dry it thoroughly in air before microscopy.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: If the fixing alcohol contains water, the cells are not fixed in the proper shape.
For the differential count the pH of the buffered water must be 6.8–7.2.
In a thick, uneven film the cells are hard to describe: the red cells are altered and the leukocytes gather at the edges.
A badly made, badly fixed or badly stained film is the main cause of errors in recognising cells.

slides.title: Quality control
bullets: The laboratory needs control films from healthy people and from patients with various pathologies.
If a film shows a lot of pathology, a second experienced worker re-examines it to confirm the findings; the result goes to the treating physician only after confirmation.
Automatic devices for making and staining films help to standardise conditions and improve the quality of preparations.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: A drying film must be kept in a safe place until it is fixed, so that it does not become contaminated.
Blood is taken in rubber gloves with a single-use lancet; all specimens are treated as potentially infectious.
